notes.short: Hearts, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, hearts
notes.about: Three words go out in one order and come back in the reverse order: hearts, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, hearts.

lines.words: Make the hearts of this people calloused;
deafen their ears
and close their eyes.
Otherwise they might see with their eyes,
hear with their ears,
understand with their hearts,

defined.quote: The Repetition of the same Words in an inverse Order (but same Sense)
defined.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

original.note: In Hebrew the ears and the eyes are the same words both times; the heart is lev, then its fuller form, levav.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists this verse under Epanodos, the same words repeated in inverse order, and again under introverted parallelism. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) and Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) both point out the reversed order. Fausset, following Bengel, reads it as corruption flowing from the heart into the ears and eyes, and healing reaching the heart through them.
notes.limit: Writers agree the order is reversed; what the reversal means is one reading, not a settled one.

cites.quote: After two, three, or more words have been mentioned, they are repeated, not in the same order again, but backward.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: In the first member of the sentence, the order is, the heart, ears, eyes; in the latter, the reverse order, the eyes, ears, heart. It is from the heart that corruption flows into the ears and eyes (Mar 7:21-22); but through the eyes and ears healing reaches the heart (Rom 10:17), [BENGEL]
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The three future clauses, with "lest" (pen), point back to these three imperatives in inverse order

notes.short: Wounds no one has dressed
notes.about: Isaiah speaks of the nation as one body, wounded from the sole of the foot to the head. Its wounds have not been cleansed, bandaged or soothed with oil: nothing has been done to heal it, and the people are left without relief.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil
figure.means: Nothing has been done to heal the nation, pictured as a wounded body: it is left without relief or remedy.

notes.evidence: Calvin calls the three phrases metaphors, all meaning the nation is left without relief or remedy. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sees the nation as one diseased body, with nothing applied to heal its wounds. Barnes: nothing was done toward healing, and the whole figure pictures the nation punished for its sins. Henry likens its sin to a diseased body: its unclosed wounds show no reform was tried.
notes.limit: Some take the wounds as the punishments the nation had already suffered, others as its sins left unrepented. Either way the picture shows a people no one has healed.

cites.quote: the three metaphors which he joins together ... have all the same meaning that the nation, without any hope of relief, without comfort, without remedy, is reduced to such a state of distress, that in such punishments the utmost severity of God is openly displayed.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This description of the total misery of every individual in the nation is followed by a representation of the whole nation as one miserably diseased body. ... no means whatever had been applied to heal these many, various wounds
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The meaning is, that nothing had been done toward healing the wound. It was an unhealed, undressed, all-pervading sore. ... The whole figure in these two verses relates to their being punished for their sins.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: How he illustrates it by a comparison taken from a sick and diseased body, all overspread with leprosy ... No attempts were made for reformation, or, if they were, they proved ineffectual: The wounds have not been closed, not bound up, nor mollified with ointment.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Holy, holy, holy”: one word said three times
notes.about: The seraphim call out “holy” three times in a row. The repetition gives the word its fullest weight: the LORD is holy beyond measure, supremely holy. It can also be heard as praise that never tires, since His holiness gives it endless cause.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.words: Holy, holy, holy
figure.means: holiness of the highest degree, and praise of it that never ceases

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis: the LORD's holiness is stressed beyond measure, to the highest degree, and he sees the three Persons indicated. Barnes says the Hebrews repeated a word for the highest degree, so the words mean supremely holy. Henry hears the angels' fervent zeal and the surpassing excellence of God's holiness. Calvin reads it as the angels' unwearied, unceasing praise.
notes.limit: The writers stress different things: holiness beyond measure, or praise that never stops. Most of them also hear the three Persons of God in the threefold praise, though some say this verse alone does not prove it; the note does not rest on that.

cites.quote: The holiness of Jehovah is emphasized beyond measure, and the three persons in one God are indicated by the thrice repeated ... Here the highest degree of holiness is ascribed to Jehovah.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The Hebrews usually expressed the superlative degree by the repetition of a word. ... The form was used, therefore, among the Jews, to denote “emphasis;” and the expression means in itself no more than ‘thrice holy;’ that is, supremely holy.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: God's power was spoken twice ... but his holiness thrice, Holy, holy, holy. This bespeaks, [1.] The zeal and fervency of the angels in praising God; they even want words to express themselves, and therefore repeat the same again. ... [3.] The superlative excellency of God's holiness, above that of the purest creatures. He is holy, thrice holy, infinitely holy
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: And, indeed, this repetition rather points out unwearied perseverance, as if the Prophet had said, that the angels never cease from their melody in singing the praises of God, as the holiness of God supplies us with inexhaustible reasons for them.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “All flesh is like grass”: frail and soon gone
notes.about: All mankind is called grass, and all its glory is likened to the flowers of the field. As grass withers and flowers fall, so people, with all their gifts and beauty, pass away. Verse 7 says it plainly: “the people are grass.” Against them stands the word of our God, which lasts forever (verse 8).

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: All flesh is like grass
figure.means: all people, weak and short-lived, who wither as grass does

original.note: In Hebrew the first line has no word for like; it says all flesh is grass. The second line has like, and Peter's Greek has it in both lines (1 Peter 1:24).

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets Peter's simile, all flesh as grass, beside Isaiah's metaphor, all flesh is grass. Barnes says all people are as weak and feeble as grass soon withered; Henry, that all flesh is grass, weak and withering, and its beauty soon blasted; Delitzsch, that men in the flesh are weak and perishing; Calvin, that man with all his gifts is compared to a flower that soon fades.
notes.limit: The writers read it of all mankind but apply it differently here: to Israel's oppressors, to Israel itself, or to no one nation in particular.

cites.quote: While the Simile says “All flesh is AS grass” (1Pe 1:24 ), the Metaphor carries the figure across at once, and says “All flesh IS grass” (Isa 40:6 ).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he states that all people are weak and feeble like the grass that is soon withered. ... Is grass - It is as feeble, weak, and as easily consumed as the grass of the field.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Of the vanity of the creature, that all flesh is grass, weak and withering. We ourselves are so, and therefore cannot save ourselves; all our friends are so, and therefore are unable to save us. All the beauty of the creature, which might render it amiable, is but as the flower of grass, soon blasted
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The appointed theme of his proclamation is the perishable nature of all flesh ... Men living in the flesh are universally impotent, perishing, limited ... Surely grass is the human race; such grass withereth and such flower fadeth
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We ought carefully to observe that man, with his faculties, on account of which he is accustomed to value himself so highly, is wholly compared to a flower. ... But he shews that in man there is nothing so excellent as not to fade quickly and perish.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Know and understood around heard and declared
notes.about: Four questions go out and come back. The first and last ask about knowing and understanding, what can be learned by thinking on what God has made; the two in the middle ask about what had been heard and declared from the beginning.

lines.words: Do you not know?
Have you not heard?
Has it not been declared to you from the beginning?
Have you not understood since the foundation of the earth?

original.note: In Hebrew the first two verbs are futures, of what could be known, and the last two are perfects, of what has in fact been so.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls these four questions chiastically arranged: God may be known by reasoning or learned by what is handed down, and Israel shut itself off from both, from the knowledge open to it in a natural way and from the teaching that had come down from the beginning of its history.
notes.limit: The last question can also be read as insight into how the earth was founded; the BSB reads it as a time. Either way, know and understood stand around heard and declared.

cites.quote: four questions chiastically arranged. The absolute being of God … may be either inferred per ratiocinationem, or learned per traditionem. When Israel failed to acknowledge the absolute distinctness and unequalled supremacy of Jehovah its God, it hardened itself against the knowledge which it might acquire even in a natural way … and shut its ears against the teaching of revelation and tradition
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “The arm of the LORD” stands for His power
notes.about: The LORD's arm stands for His power, the strength by which He acts. Here it is His saving power, made known in the Servant this chapter describes, yet few have seen it. John 12:38 applies the verse to the many who did not believe in Jesus.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: the arm of the LORD
figure.means: the LORD's power, here His saving power made known in grace

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: the LORD's arm makes known His grace in power. Barnes: the arm, an emblem of power, is God's power shown through the Messiah. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): power, shown in miracles and in saving men. Henry: the divine power that goes with the word. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): almighty power that saves His people and exalts the Servant.
notes.limit: The writers agree the arm is God's power. They differ on where it is seen most: in the miracles that confirmed Christ's teaching, in the saving of sinners, or in the raising up of the Servant.

cites.quote: The Arm of the Lord is also used of the making known of His grace in wondrous power.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The arm is that by which we execute a purpose, and is often used as the emblem of power ... Here it denotes the omnipotence or power of God, which would be exhibited through the Messiah.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: arm--power ... exercised in miracles and in saving men ... "The arm of Jehovah" exhibited in Messiah while on earth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the arm of the Lord is not revealed to them; they do not discern, nor will be brought to acknowledge, that divine power which goes along with the word. The arm of the Lord is made bare ... in the miracles that were wrought to confirm Christ's doctrine
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: the "arm of Jehovah," namely, His holy arm that has been made bare, and that now effects the salvation of His people, and of the nations generally ... who has recognised the omnipotence of Jehovah, which has set itself to effect his exaltation?
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “We all like sheep have gone astray”
notes.about: The speakers confess that they are like sheep that have wandered off, each one turning to his own way. Sheep stray easily and cannot find the way home; so all had left God. The same verse says the LORD laid their iniquity on Him. Peter takes up the picture in 1 Peter 2:25.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: We all like sheep have gone astray
figure.means: people who have wandered from God, like sheep without a shepherd, each going his own way

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives these words as his example of a simile. Barnes says the race without a Redeemer is compared to a flock without a shepherd that wanders into every danger; Delitzsch, that Israel resembled a scattered flock without a shepherd; Henry, that we are like sheep, apt to wander and unable to find the way home.

cites.quote: The Simile says “All we like sheep,” while the Metaphor declares that “we are the sheep of His pasture.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The condition of the race without a Redeemer is here elegantly compared to a flock without a shepherd, which wanders where it chooses, and which is exposed to all dangers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Israel in its exile resembled a scattered flock without a shepherd; it had lost the way of Jehovah
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We have gone astray like sheep, which are apt to wander, and are unapt, when they have gone astray, to find the way home again. That is our true character
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Silent “as a sheep before her shearers”
notes.about: The Servant is compared to a lamb led to be killed and to a sheep silent before its shearers. Like them He goes without resisting or complaining, and does not open His mouth. In Acts 8:32-35 Philip begins from this passage to tell the good news about Jesus.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent
figure.means: the Servant's willing, quiet bearing as He suffers, with no word of complaint

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among his similes built on as and so. Delitzsch says the first simile shows His willing endurance and the second His quiet submission. Barnes: as a lamb led to be killed is patient and silent, so was He; Henry: His patience, His meekness and His cheerful yielding to His Father's will.

cites.quote: suffered; Lamb dumb, and so He; etc. (Isa 53:7 )
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The voluntary endurance is then explained by the simile "like a sheep that is led to the slaughter" (an attributive clause, like Jer 11:19 ); and the submissive quiet bearing, by the simile "like a lamb that is dumb before its shearers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This does not mean that he was led to the slaughter as a lamb is, but that as a lamb which is led to be killed is patient and silent, so was he. He made no resistance. ... As a sheep submits quietly to the operation of shearing.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: and as a sheep is dumb before the shearers, nay, before the butchers, so he opened not his mouth, which denotes not only his exemplary patience under affliction ... and his meekness under reproach ... but his cheerful compliance with his Father's will.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Thoughts, ways, then ways, thoughts
notes.about: Two words go out in one order and come back in the reverse order: thoughts, then ways in verse 8; ways, then thoughts in verse 9. Within verse 8, My and your also go out and come back reversed.

lines.words: For My thoughts are not your thoughts,
neither are your ways My ways,
For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways
and My thoughts than your thoughts.

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets out verse 8 as My thoughts, your thoughts, your ways, My ways, and says that verses 8 and 9 taken together are a simple Epanodos, the same words repeated in reverse order: thoughts, ways, ways, thoughts.

cites.quote: a “For my thoughts b are not your thoughts, b neither are your ways a my ways, saith the Lord.” … In verses 8 and 9 taken together, the figure is a simple Epanodos … Here in a and a we have “thoughts”; while in b and b we have “ways.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Mountains sing and trees clap their hands
notes.about: The mountains and hills are pictured singing, and the trees clapping their hands, as people do for joy. It shows the great joy of God's people as they go out and are led forth in peace. Some also read in it all creation sharing their freedom (Romans 8:21). Psalm 98:8 has a like picture.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: the mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands
figure.means: the great joy of God's people as they go out and are led forth in peace, as if all nature shared it

original.note: In Hebrew “hands” is kaph; in giving the trees hands, the prophet may have had in mind their branches, kippot.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Personification. Albert Barnes: lifeless things are pictured sharing the joy of God's people. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): nature's seeming sympathy, and its renewal. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): the shouting and clapping are not literal, and creation will share the freedom of God's children. Plumptre (Ellicott): waving branches are like clapping hands.
notes.limit: All read the words as a picture of joy. Two also see in them the whole creation one day set free with God's people; the others do not say so.

cites.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to inanimate things, p. 866
cites.quote: “The mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.” And thus is emphasised the universal joy of Israel in the coming day of her glory, when Jehovah shall comfort her.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Language like this is common in Isaiah, where all nature is called on to rejoice, or where inanimate objects are represented as expressing their sympathy with the joy of the people of God … Here it is an expression of the universal rejoicing which would attend the extension of the kingdom of God on the earth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: images justly used to express the seeming sympathy of nature with the joy of God's people. For, when sin is removed, the natural world shall be delivered from "vanity," and be renewed, so as to be in unison with the regenerated moral world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In applying the term kaph (hand) to the trees, the prophet had in his mind their kippōth, or branches. … That this transformation of the vegetation of the desert is not to be taken literally … is evident from the shouting of the mountains, and the clapping of hands on the part of the trees. … the whole creation will one day share in the liberty and glory of the children of God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The waving of the branches of the trees is, in the poet’s thoughts, what the clapping of hands is with men, a sign of jubilant exultation
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Your people possessed it; our enemies trample it
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. For a short while God's own people possessed His holy place; now enemies have trampled His sanctuary. The prayer sets the two side by side as a plea for God to act.

lines.words: For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place,
but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary.

original.note: In Hebrew the second line turns the order round, so the two very different subjects, Your people and our enemies, meet in the middle of the verse.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words of the two clauses stand in reverse order, so that their two very different subjects touch in the middle, and the first verb looks further back than the second. Albert Barnes reads the verse as a plea: God's people possessed His sanctuary only a little time, and now His enemies trample it down.
notes.limit: What God's people held for a short while can be read as the holy land or as the temple itself.

cites.quote: The order of the words in the two clauses is chiastic. The two strikingly different subjects touch one another as the two inner members. Of the perfects, the first expresses the more remote past, the second the nearer past
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As a reason for this, we urge that thy temple thy holy sanctuary - was possessed by thy people but a little time. For a brief period there we offered praise, and met with our God, and enjoyed his favor. Now thine enemies trample it down.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Heaven and earth are called on to listen
notes.about: Isaiah turns from the people and calls on the heavens and the earth to listen, as if they could hear the LORD's charge against His children. Some read it as a rebuke: the lifeless creation will listen sooner than God's own people.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
figure.means: heaven and earth, called as if they could hear, to witness the LORD's charge against His rebellious children

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Apostrophe to inanimate things. Calvin says the prophet turns to the dumb and lifeless elements because men have no ears. Henry says the prophet, despairing of a hearing from his people, speaks to the heavens and the earth. Barnes says heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses, in high poetic language that marks the weight of the matter.
notes.limit: One writer also offers a reading of heaven and earth as angels and the people of the world; others reject that reading and take them as the heavens and the earth themselves.

cites.quote: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the Lord hath spoken.” These words were chosen for, and invariably put in, the title-page of the early printed editions of the English Bible.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is unquestionably a very severe protestation; for it conveys this meaning, that both turn to the elements which are dumb and devoid of feeling, because men have now no ears, or are bereft of all their senses. ... That no one may wonder at the circumstance of his addressing dumb and lifeless objects
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The prophet, though he speaks in God's name, yet, despairing to gain audience with the children of his people, addresses himself to the heavens and the earth, and bespeaks their attention ... Sooner will the inanimate creatures hear, who observe the law and answer the end of their creation, than this stupid senseless people.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The heavens and the earth are summoned to bear witness to the apostasy, ingratitude, and deep depravity of the chosen people of God. ... It is high poetic language, denoting the importance of the subject, and the remarkable and amazing truth to which the attention was to be called.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Israel does not know: they do not understand
notes.about: The second line says the first again and explains it. Israel does not know, and the next line tells what that means: God's people do not understand.

lines.words: but Israel does not know;
My people do not understand.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Cause, among verbs, and says the next parallel line explains the words Israel does not know. He adds that it also comes under Exergasia.

cites.quote: “Israel doth not know.” The next parallel line goes on to explain it:-“My people doth not consider.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: The ox and donkey know; Israel does not
notes.about: The lines take turns. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger; Israel does not know, and God's people do not understand. What Israel fails to know answers to the owner, and what it fails to understand answers to the manger: even the beasts know more than God's people.

lines.words: The ox knows its owner,
and the donkey its master’s manger,
but Israel does not know;
My people do not understand.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the parallel requires that Israel does not know its Owner, and that not considering answers to the crib in the parallel clause. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) supplies the objects from the lines before: Israel did not know or consider what answered to the owner and to the crib, and so fell below the beasts.

cites.quote: not know--namely, his Owner, as the parallelism requires; that is, not recognize Him as such ( Exo 19:5 , equivalent to "my people," Joh 1:10-11 ). consider--attend to his Master ( Isa 41:8 ), notwithstanding the spiritual food which He provides (answering to "crib" in the parallel clause).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Jehovah then complains that the rebellion with which His children have rewarded Him is not only inhuman, but even worse than that of the brutes ... the object is to be supplied from what goes before: they knew not, and did not consider what answered in their case to the owner and to the crib which the master fills
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Alas”: the prophet cries out over a sinful nation
notes.about: After charging the people in plain words, Isaiah cries out, “Alas, O sinful nation,” and heaps up names for a people weighed down by sin. Many hear in the cry both sorrow and indignation, for the people have forsaken the LORD and despised the Holy One of Israel.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: Alas, O sinful nation
figure.means: sorrow and indignation at a people who have forsaken the LORD

original.note: In Hebrew “Alas” is hoy, a cry of pain that can also carry anger.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ecphonesis, or Exclamation. Calvin calls it an exclamation of astonishment and sorrow that voices abhorrence; Henry says the prophet bemoans the people with holy indignation; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls hoy a cry of pain, here a lament filled with wrath; Plumptre (Ellicott) hears in it indignation rather than pity.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the cry's chief note: most hear grief joined with indignation, but one hears indignation rather than pity.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) takes the spirit to be the wisdom Egypt was famed for, answering to counsel in the parallel clause. John Calvin says the word means understanding here, and that the added words on destroying their counsel are a stronger expression of the former statement, showing the cause of that emptiness.

cites.quote: spirit--wisdom, for which Egypt was famed ( Isa 31:2 ; Kg1 4:30 ; Act 7:22 ); answering to "counsel" in the parallel clause.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Consequently, רוח (rūăch) means here understanding and sagacity, which ought to be carefully observed, for many are mistaken as to the meaning of this word. When he immediately adds, I will destroy the counsel thereof, this is a stronger expression of the former statement; for it shews what is the cause of that emptiness, namely, that God will take and carry away their counsel.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Harsh masters, a fierce king
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: the harsh masters the Egyptians are handed over to and the fierce king who will rule over them are one and the same. Read this way, one ruler is meant.

lines.words: I will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of harsh masters,
and a fierce king will rule over them,

original.note: In Hebrew the word for masters is plural, a form often used for one great lord, while the king in the next line is singular.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the word for lord is plural in Hebrew but is applied to a single monarch, since the parallel member names a fierce king in the singular, which evidently denotes the same. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the plural expresses greatness where one alone is meant, and the parallel word king proves it.
notes.limit: The note does not say who this ruler was; the writers differ on which king is meant.

cites.quote: The word rendered 'lord,' meaning master, is in the Hebrew in the plural number ... In the parallel member, also, a name in the singular number is used - 'a fierce king;' and as this evidently denotes the same, it follows that the word here is used to denote a single monarch.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: in Hebrew it is lords; but plural is often used to express greatness, where, one alone is meant ( Gen 39:2 ). The parallel word "king" (singular) proves it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The Nile dries up, its riverbed parched
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: the waters that dry up and the riverbed left parched and empty are both the Nile.

lines.words: The waters of the Nile will dry up,
and the riverbed will be parched and empty.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line says the waters will dry up from the sea, a name the Nile was often given, and the second line calls it the river.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the parallelism and the whole scope of the passage require the sea here to be the Nile, which is often called a sea, and he takes the river in the next line as the Nile too.

cites.quote: From the sea - The parallelism here, as well as the whole scope of the passage, requires us to understand this of the Nile. The word ים yâm is sometimes used to denote a large river (see the notes at Isa 11:15 ; Isa 18:2 ). The Nile is often called a sea. ... And the river - The Nile.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: An altar and a pillar to the LORD
notes.about: The second line answers the first and explains it: the pillar shows what kind of altar is meant, a memorial and a place of worship. Both mark that the LORD will be worshiped in Egypt.

lines.words: In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the center of the land of Egypt,
and a pillar to the LORD near her border.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the parallelism, where pillars are mentioned, shows in what sense the altar is meant, a place of memorial or of worship in general, so that the worship of the true God would be set up in Egypt. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the altar is not for sacrifice but, like the pillar, for memorial and worship.

cites.quote: But the word 'altar' is often used in another sense to denote a place of "memorial;" or a place of worship in general ... The parallelism here, where 'pillars' are mentioned, shows in what sense the word 'altar' is used. It means that the worship of the true God would be established in Egypt
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: altar--not for sacrifice, but as the "pillar" for memorial and worship
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Isaiah goes naked and barefoot as a sign
notes.about: The LORD tells Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals, and he walks about naked and barefoot. Verse 3 calls this “a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush”: in the same way Assyria would lead their people away as captives, stripped and barefoot, and all who trusted in Egypt would be ashamed.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: walking around naked and barefoot
figure.means: Egypt and Cush would be stripped of all they had and led away captive by Assyria, as verses 3 and 4 explain

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it the making of Isaiah a sign of Egypt and Cush led away stripped. John Calvin says the LORD confirmed the prophecy by a visible symbol. Albert Barnes calls his laying aside his garment an emblem of Egypt stripped of its possessions. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says his strange dress foretold the fall of Egypt and Cush.
notes.limit: These writers read naked as without his outer garment, not wholly unclothed. They differ on the three years: whether he went this way whenever he spoke as a prophet over three years, or the sign pointed to three years of trouble for Egypt and Cush.

cites.quote: The making of Isaiah a sign, by his unusual dress when he walked abroad. ... The hearts of that people were strangely stupid, and would not be affected with what they only heard, but must be taught by signs ... It was intended to signify that the Egyptians and the Ethiopians should be led away captive by the king of Assyria, thus stripped, or in rags, and very shabby clothing, as Isaiah was.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In order to confirm this prophecy by the use of a symbol, the Lord commanded Isaiah to walk naked. ... He places himself in the midst between God and his countrymen, so as to be the herald of a future calamity, not only in words, but likewise by a visible symbol.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: His removing this garment was designed to be a sign or an emblem to show that the Egyptians should be stripped of all their possessions, and carried captive to Assyria. ... The prophets were accustomed to use symbolic actions to denote the events which they foretold
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The expression "as he goeth" (ca'asher hâlac) stands here at the commencement of the symbolical action ... The strange and unseemly dress of the prophet, whenever he appeared in his official capacity for three whole years, was a prediction of the fall of the Egypto-Ethiopian kingdom, which was to take place at the end of these three years.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The watchman's dark answer: morning, then night
notes.about: Someone from Seir, the land of Edom, asks the watchman twice how much of the night is left. The answer is short and dark: “Morning has come, but also the night.” Many read it as a dawn of relief followed by a night of trouble, and the asker is told to inquire and come back.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.words: Morning has come, but also the night.
figure.means: a morning of relief and a night of trouble both coming, so that the asker is given no lasting comfort

original.note: In Hebrew the answer is given in an Aramaic form of the language, with atah for come and ba'ah for inquire.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists both verses under Ænigma as another dark saying. Barnes calls the prophecy brief, enigmatical and obscure, and Henry short and dark; Barnes takes the morning as deliverance for the Jews and the night as calamity for Edom, Henry as peace before trouble. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): the reply lets the asker see darkly, in Aramaic form; each dawn for Edom is swallowed by night.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whom the morning and the night fall: one takes the morning for the Jews and the night for Edom, others take both as coming to Edom in turn.

cites.quote: Isa 21:11-12, is another dark saying.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The 'morning' here is an emblem of prosperity ... This refers to the deliverance from the captivity of Babylon ... 'The morning cometh' - to the captive Jews; 'and also the night' - to some other people - to wit, the Idumeans. ... And also the night - A time of calamity and affliction. ... This seems to be the sense of this very dark and difficult prophecy. It is brief, enigmatical, and obscure.

cites.quote: This prophecy concerning Dumah is very short, and withal dark and hard to be understood. ... There comes first a morning of light, and peace, and opportunity; you will enjoy one day of comfort more; but afterwards comes a night of trouble and calamity.

notes.short: Praise in the east and in the islands of the sea
notes.about: Both lines give one call to praise in other words: glorify becomes extol, and the east is answered by the islands of the sea in the west. Together they call for praise from the east to the west.

lines.words: Therefore glorify the LORD in the east.
Extol the name of the LORD, the God of Israel in the islands of the sea.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says the parallelism demands that the first place be a region of light, where the sun rises, so that the verse calls the scattered people to glorify God in the East and in the West. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) takes the islands as the coastlands of the west and the other word as the lands of the sunrise, and says the appeal goes out both east and west.
notes.limit: The Hebrew word the BSB gives as the east is rare, and some render it fires or valleys instead; read that way, the two places do not answer each other as east and west.

cites.quote: The word probably refers either to the regions of the morning light, the rising of the sun ... The parallelism, the construction, demands such an interpretation. It would then be equivalent to calling on the scattered people to glorify God in the East, and in the West; in the regions of the rising sun and in the coasts of the sea; or wherever they were scattered.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Turning in that direction, it had the islands and coast lands of the European West in front ... and at its back the lands of the Asiatic East, which are called 'urim, the lands of light, i.e., of the sun-rising. ... the beauty of the appeal, which goes forth both to the east and west, and summons to the praise of the name of Jehovah the God of Israel
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The host of heaven above, the kings of earth below
notes.about: The lines set heaven against earth: the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below. Many read the contrast as showing that the host of heaven means powers in the spiritual world, judged along with the rulers of the earth.

lines.words: the host of heaven above
and the kings of the earth below

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) says the antithetical parallelism of the clauses rules out taking the high ones as mere earthly kingdoms. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) points to the twice-stated antithesis of height and earth, and says the parallelism shows a judgment in the spiritual world. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the antithesis shows unseen rulers.
notes.limit: Some read the second line as explaining the first, taking the host of heaven as the rulers of the earth, who shine like stars; the lines would then say one thing twice.

cites.quote: Jehovah visits also the “principalities and powers in heavenly places” ( Eph 3:10 ) or “on high” ( Eph 6:12 ). ... The antithetical parallelism of the two clauses is decisive against the interpretation which sees in the “high ones on high” only the representatives of earthly kingdoms
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: With this doubly expressed antithesis of mârōm and 'adâmâh (cf., Isa 23:17 ) before us, brought out as it is as sharply as possible, we cannot understand "the army of the high place" as referring to certain earthly powers ... Both the context and the parallelism show that the reference must be to a penal visitation in the spiritual world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: host of . . . high ones--the heavenly host, that is, either the visible host of heaven ... or rather, "the invisible rulers of the darkness of this world," as the antithesis to "kings of the earth" shows.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Uproar subdued, the song of the ruthless silenced
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: God subdues the uproar of foreigners, and the song of the ruthless is silenced. The heat cooled by the shade of a cloud pictures how He checks their fury.

lines.words: You subdue the uproar of foreigners.
As the shade of a cloud cools the heat, so the song of the ruthless is silenced.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says the parallelism requires the shadow of a cloud to be understood in the first half as well, and sets the halves side by side: the noise of the strangers humbled, the exultation of the formidable ones brought low. John Calvin says the last clause confirms the statement before it, that the shouting of the wicked will be laid low as heat is overpowered.

cites.quote: The parallelism here requires that we should suppose the phrase 'with the shadow of a cloud' to be supplied in this hemistich ... The noise of the strangers shalt thou humble; As the heat by the shadow of a cloud, The exultation of the formidable ones shalt thou bring low.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He therefore confirms the preceding statement, that the violence of wicked men, or the shouting which they haughtily and daringly set up, will presently be laid low, as the heat of the sun is overpowered by the falling rain, which is meant by the shadow of a cloud
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Waiting in God's ways, longing for His name
notes.about: The lines answer each other: waiting for the LORD in the path of His judgments is matched by the soul's desire for His name and renown. Read this way, His judgments can mean His laws, kept by people who long for Him.

lines.words: Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments.
Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) takes the judgments here as God's laws, because in the corresponding member of the parallelism the people say their soul's desire is to God and to the remembrance of Him, which implies they sought to please Him by keeping His laws.
notes.limit: Others take His judgments here as the trials He sends, or His coming to judge, rather than His laws.

cites.quote: The word 'judgments' often refers to the statutes or laws of God. ... I am inclined to the belief that this is the true interpretation, because in the corresponding member of the parallelism they are represented as saying that the desire of their soul was to God, and to the remembrance of him, implying that they sought by an observance of his laws to please him, and to secure his favor.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Judgments teach righteousness; grace alone does not
notes.about: The two lines are set against each other: when God's judgments come, the people of the world learn righteousness, but when grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn it. The contrast can show why judgment is needed, since favour alone does not teach him.

lines.words: For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness.
Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness.

notes.evidence: John Calvin says Isaiah contrasts this statement with the one before: the earth owns God's justice when He judges, but the wicked are not won to love Him by any kindness. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) says verse 10 shows the thought of verse 9 from another side: judgments teach evildoers, while under mere favour they stay as they are.

cites.quote: Isaiah contrasts this statement with the former. ... But now he declares, on the other hand, that the wicked cannot be brought in any way to love God, though he endeavor, by every sort of kindness ... This verse appears, at first view, to contradict the former, in which the Prophet said, that the justice of God is acknowledged in the earth, when he executes his judgments
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The thought of Isa 26:9 is presented under another aspect. The judgments of God manifested against evil are the only discipline by which the doers of evil can be taught ... under a system of mere tolerance and favour, they remain as they are.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A nation enlarged, its borders extended
notes.about: The last line explains the first: the LORD has enlarged the nation, and He has extended all the borders of the land. Both lines speak of one increase of His people, which brings Him glory.

lines.words: You have enlarged the nation, O LORD
You have extended all the borders of the land.

notes.evidence: John Calvin views the two statements as closely connected and says the latter clause is an interpretation of the former: God has increased His people and extended His kingdom. Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) renders the last line as extending far all the borders of the land, and says the parallelism requires this construction.
notes.limit: An older rendering of the last line spoke of the people removed far away, to the ends of the earth; read that way, it does not answer the first line.

cites.quote: But when I attend to what follows, Thou hast enlarged, that is, “Thou hast extended thy kingdom, which formerly was confined within narrow limits,” I choose rather to view the two statements as closely connected; for the latter clause is an interpretation of the former.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Or rather, thou hast extended far all the borders of the land. ... The parallelism requires this construction, and it is indeed the obvious one
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Sought in distress, a quiet prayer under discipline
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: their distress is answered by the LORD's discipline, and seeking Him is answered by pouring out a quiet prayer.

lines.words: O LORD, they sought You in their distress;
when You disciplined them, they poured out a quiet prayer.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says that in the parallel line the clause about the LORD's chastening corresponds to the words in trouble, and the whispered prayer poured out answers to the word for seeking Him.

cites.quote: Jehovah, in trouble they missed Thee, poured out light supplication when Thy chastisement came upon them. ... The substantive circumstantial clause in the parallel line, למו מוּסר, castigatione tua eos affilgente (ל as in Isa 26:9 ), corresponds to בּצּר; and לחשׁ צקוּן, ... answers to pâkad

notes.short: Leviathan, the serpent, the dragon: one enemy
notes.about: The verse names the enemy three times: Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the coiling serpent, and the dragon of the sea. Each phrase can be read as naming the same enemy of God's people again, under another picture.

lines.words: bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent
Leviathan the coiling serpent
and He will slay the dragon of the sea.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) holds that the verse speaks not of different enemies but of the same one, since Hebrew poetry names one subject in different members of a sentence, and calls the dragon the same thing under another image. Matthew Poole (Poole's Annotations) takes the words as metaphor and says leviathan, serpent and dragon all signify the same thing, a very powerful enemy or enemies.
notes.limit: Other writers read the three names as three different powers, such as Assyria, Babylon and Egypt. Which enemy is meant is not settled.

cites.quote: The reference in Isaiah, I suppose, is not to "different" kings or enemies of the people of God, but to the same. It is customary in Hebrew poetry to refer to the same subject in different members of the same sentence, or in different parts of the same parallelism. The dragon - Referring to the same thing under a different image - to the king of Babylon.

cites.quote: But here it is certain that the expression is metaphorical, and that by this leviathan, serpent, and dragon (for all signify the same thing) he understands some very powerful enemy or enemies

notes.short: A song of the LORD's well-kept vineyard
notes.about: A short song pictures God's people as a fruitful vineyard. The LORD Himself is its keeper: He waters it and guards it night and day, and if thorns and briers confronted Him He would burn them. Verse 6 then says plainly whom the picture means: “Jacob will take root.”

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Sing about a fruitful vineyard
figure.means: God's people, whom the LORD keeps, waters and guards; verse 6 names them Jacob and Israel

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls it a song about Judea, pictured as a vineyard. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the vineyard is a symbol of Israel and the thorns and thistles a figure for the enemies of the church. John Calvin says the figure of the vineyard speaks more strongly than naming Israel would, and shows God's love for His Church.
notes.limit: One of these writers ends the song at verse 5 and takes verse 6 as its explanation; another carries it to the end of the chapter. They name the vineyard as Judea, Israel or the church.

cites.quote: Sing ye unto her - That is, sing unto, or respecting the vineyard. ... It is the commencement of a song, or hymn respecting Judea, represented under the image of a vineyard

notes.short: A bed too short: their safety will give no rest
notes.about: The rulers of Jerusalem boasted, “We have made a covenant with death.” Most of the writers read verse 20 as a picture of that false safety: a bed too short to stretch out on, a blanket too small to wrap in. What they trusted would give them neither rest nor cover when judgment came.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the bed is too short to stretch out on
figure.means: the false safety the rulers trusted in, which would give them no rest and no cover when the scourge came

Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) applies the figure to the treaty in which they thought they had rest and safety; Calvin calls it a metaphor: like men hidden in a short bed, they find pain, not rest; Barnes and Henry say their refuges would fail.
notes.limit: Two of these writers think the words were a proverbial saying. They differ on what the rulers trusted in: one names the treaty with Egypt, another idols and false prophets as well.

notes.short: A farmer's ways picture God's measured dealings
notes.about: After a call to listen, Isaiah asks about a farmer's work. He does not plow forever, sows each seed in its place, and threshes each crop with the right tool without crushing it. His skill is from the LORD. Most read it as a picture of how God deals with His people: in measure, not to destroy.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Does the plowman plow for planting every day?
figure.means: God's dealings with His people: as the farmer does not plow or thresh without end, God punishes in measure and for a time, to bring a harvest

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it a parable from the farmer's calling, the threshing being afflictions measured to our strength. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a parable: the farmer's course is a type of God's dealings with Israel, whom He punishes in order to bless. Albert Barnes, an allegory: God varies His ways as a farmer does. John Calvin says it explains God's judgments by metaphors.

notes.short: A grave with the wicked, yet with a rich man
notes.about: The two lines are set against each other. He was assigned a grave with the wicked, but in His death He was with a rich man. What men intended is set against what came to pass, which many see fulfilled when a rich man laid His body in his own new tomb.

lines.words: He was assigned a grave with the wicked,
and with a rich man in His death,

original.note: In Hebrew the word for a rich man means one who is rich, never by itself one who is wicked, so the second line does not simply repeat the first.

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the parallel one of contrast, between men's design and the fact as God ordered it. Albert Barnes reads the and as but: He was to be buried with the wicked, but was with the rich. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) finds a contrast of a rich man and a criminal: the first clause gives the grave first assigned, the second the one after His death.
notes.limit: Some have taken the rich man as another name for the wicked, so that the second line would say the first again; the cited writers reject that reading.

cites.quote: rather, "but He was with a rich man," &c. ... the Hebrew everywhere means "rich," never by itself ungodly; the parallelism, too, is one of contrast; namely, between their design and the fact, as it was ordered by God
